card.hook: Picture a giant crab waving its claws above a canal, with a whole wall of neon doubled in the water below it. That's Dōtonbori after dark, and your phone will love it.
card.stand_here: Stand near とんぼり, about 15 m south-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-east. A few steps either side lets you change the angle.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the whole street scene. Go to 0.5x to squeeze tall signs and the canal into one shot, then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for a single sign or lantern.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the brightest sign, then drag the slider down to darker so the lights keep their colour instead of washing out to white.
card.best_time: Go after dark, when the signs are lit and glow in the canal. It's busiest in the evening, so earlier in the evening gives you a clearer view.
card.selfie_here: Head down the steps from Ebisubashi Bridge to the Tombori River Walk on the south bank. It's much quieter than the bridge, and you can frame the sign against its reflection in the canal. Use the front camera at 0.5x and keep the signs over your shoulder. Daytime selfies come out sharper, because the lights flash at night.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the sidewalk one flight of stairs down from Ebisubashi Bridge, so they can frame the whole sign behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: It's crowded here, so hold your phone steady and keep an eye on the people around you. Shops and restaurants have their own rules, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Catch the moving crab with a Live Photo, then find one sign whose reflection looks even better than the real thing.
card.good_to_know: The canal was begun in 1612 and finished in 1615. By 1662 the area had six Kabuki and five Bunraku theatres. The crab sign went up in 1996, and the canal-side walkway between Tazaemonbashi and Ebisubashi opened in 2004.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand near とんぼり, about 15 m south-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-east. A few steps either side lets you change the angle.

card.hook: From the outside, Osaka Castle's keep looks like five storeys. Inside, it's secretly eight. Luckily, the photo only has to deal with the outside, where a tall stone base and tiered keep make a shape that frames itself.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon on the map, about 65 m south of Osaka Castle, and face north. The keep rises ahead of you above its stone base.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x so the base and the top of the keep both fit from this close. Then try 1x for a more natural look, or 2x-5x (depends on your phone) for the top storeys or the stone walls.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, hold your phone upright, and tap the keep, then slide it a little darker if the sky is bright so the white walls keep their detail.
card.best_time: Go on a clear morning or afternoon. Facing north from here, the sun is usually behind you and lights up the front of the keep. Early on a weekday is likely to be quieter.
card.selfie_here: Head to the open plaza in front of the keep, reached after Sakuramon Gate, and put the tower behind you. Use the front camera at 0.5x with the castle over your shoulder. The pond in the Japanese Garden is another option: stand on the garden side so the castle's reflection is behind you, though wind can blur it.
card.ask_someone: At the wide promenade entrance of Shinshigino Bridge, a short walk from the castle, a companion can stand in front of the castle to take your photo, but it can be quiet there, so you may not find a passer-by.
card.rules_and_safety: Selfie sticks are restricted inside the castle tower and in crowded outdoor areas. Entry to the keep may be ticketed or restricted, and the Japanese Garden is a paid area, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Find a granite wall block with a family crest on it, then use it as your foreground with the whole keep rising behind it.
card.good_to_know: Toyotomi Hideyoshi began building the castle in 1583, on the site of the Ishiyama Hongan-ji temple. The stone walls from the 1620s still stand. They're made of interlocking granite blocks laid without mortar, and many carry the crests of the families who supplied them. The grounds cover roughly 61,000 square metres and are ringed by moats, so there's plenty of room to try different angles.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the phone icon on the map, about 65 m south of Osaka Castle, and face north. The keep rises ahead of you above its stone base.

card.hook: Stand at the bottom, tip your head back, and two 40-storey towers seem to be holding a bridge up in thin air. It's a very good trick for a phone photo.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the phone icon on the map, at the base of the towers in the Shin-Umeda City area, and look straight up through the gap between them. Then walk a few paces back towards the gardens for a wider view.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x so both towers and the top bridge fit in from close up. Switch to 1x for a calmer, less stretched look, then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the glass bridge and escalators.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line the towers up with the vertical lines so they stand tall and don't lean.
card.best_time: Late afternoon to dusk is lovely, when the sky is softer and the glass can pick up warm light. After dark, switch on night mode and rest your phone against a railing or wall to keep it steady.
card.selfie_here: Try the lawns on the Umekita Park side, north of the building, with the towers rising behind you. A blog says the towers look deeper from there. Use your front camera (0.5x if it has the button) and tilt it up a little so the towers sit over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand well back on the Umekita Park lawns north of the building and hold the phone upright, so the whole building fits in behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: On the rooftop Sky Walk, umbrellas, food and smoking aren't allowed, and loose hats are best left off because of the wind. Keep a firm grip on your phone near the railing and never push it out over the edge. Access and tickets can change, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take one shot where the glass bridge sits in the top third and the gap between the towers fills the middle, then take a step back and see how it changes.
card.good_to_know: The Umeda Sky Building opened to the public on 25 March 1993 and was designed by Hiroshi Hara. He wanted a "floating city", and the linked top floors do look like they hang above the gap. The towers reach 170 m, or 190 m with the spires, and the rooftop Floating Garden Observatory is the main attraction inside.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand right at the phone icon on the map, at the base of the towers in the Shin-Umeda City area, and look straight up through the gap between them. Then walk a few paces back towards the gardens for a wider view.

card.hook: You can't miss the Kuromon entrance: a big 黒門 lantern hangs over a covered arcade packed with food stalls, and the whole place says "hungry? come in" before you've taken a step.
card.stand_here: Stand right in front of the market sign and lantern and face the arcade, so the colourful stalls stretch away behind them.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x so the sign, lantern and arcade all sit together. If the entrance feels cramped, try zoom 0.5x. Once you're inside, zoom 2x or more (depending on your phone) is handy for the seafood displays and stall details.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the lantern, and if the bright signs look washed out, slide the picture a touch darker.
card.best_time: We don't have a best time for this one. It's a working market, so check the official site for current opening days before you go, and take a few frames in a row because people walk through your shot all the time.
card.selfie_here: Go to the market entrance by the big 黒門 lantern, use the front camera at 0.5x, and keep the lantern and market sign over your shoulder. For a second selfie, try the giant king crab stalls inside the arcade, with the stalls behind you.
card.ask_someone: At the market entrance, hand your phone to a friendly passer-by and stand by the lantern so the colourful shop signs and the busy crowds are behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Ask before photographing a person directly (most vendors will pose if you ask politely), and don't block the walkway while you frame your shot. Step to the side first.
card.challenge: Find the seafood displays on ice and get one shot where the arcade roof and stalls frame the whole scene, with no stranger's face in it.
card.good_to_know: Kuromon Ichiba Market is a covered shopping arcade in central Osaka, lined with food stalls and small shops. It's still a working market, so vendors are busy and the aisles fill up. The big 黒門 lantern at the entrance is how most people spot they've arrived.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: From the phone icon, walk about 150 m south, roughly a couple of minutes on foot, to the main entrance of 黒門市場. Stand right in front of the market sign and lantern and face the arcade, so the colourful stalls stretch away behind them.

card.hook: Point your phone up at Abeno Harukas and the whole street seems to shrink next to it. It's so much taller than its neighbours that the tower fills the frame whether you planned for it or not.
card.stand_here: Head for the spot near アーバンアヴェニュー and stand about 50 m west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map. Face east and you get a long, upward view of the tower instead of a flat front-on shot.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole tower in, and keep your phone as upright as you can, because tilting it back makes the sides lean in. For a cleaner, more graphic shot, switch to zoom 1x on the upper floors, or try zoom 2x-5x if your phone has it to pick out the glass pattern at the top.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the sky, then slide the brightness a little darker so the sky doesn't wash out to white and the glass keeps its detail.
card.best_time: Late afternoon, when the sun is low in the west, should light the face of the tower you're looking at. Just after sunset, when the building's lights come on but the sky still has some colour, is another good moment, and night mode helps if it gets dark.
card.selfie_here: Try Lawn Square in Tennoji Park, where a guide says you can fit Abeno Harukas and another iconic Osaka landmark into one photo. You could also try the Abenohodo pedestrian bridge near the tower. Use the front camera at zoom 0.5x with the tower over your shoulder, and the bridge should make it look even taller.
card.rules_and_safety: Heading up to the Harukas 300 observatory? Drones are prohibited there, and commercial photography needs advance permission. Check the official site before you go, because the observatory, hotel and shops are separate businesses.
card.challenge: Turn on the gridlines, line the tower up with a vertical line so it stands dead straight, and see if you can get a person or a bit of street at the bottom to show off the height.
card.good_to_know: Abeno Harukas is 300 m tall with 62 floors, and it was the tallest building in Japan from 2014 to 2023. It finished on 7 March 2014, and the name comes from an old Japanese word, harukasu, meaning "to brighten, to clear up". Inside you'll find Osaka Abenobashi Station, a department store, a Marriott hotel and an observatory on the 58th to 60th floors.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for the spot near アーバンアヴェニュー and stand about 50 m west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map. Face east and you get a long, upward view of the tower instead of a flat front-on shot.

card.hook: You've been shuffling through a roofed arcade full of shoppers, and then the roof just stops. The canal opens up and a giant neon runner is waving his arms at you from across the water.
card.stand_here: Stand on Ebisubashi, the bridge at the south end of Shinsaibashi-suji where the arcade meets the Dotonbori canal. Face the Glico running man sign across the water; the arcade is behind you to the north.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the sign, the canal and the neon waterfront into one frame. Zoom 1x gives a calmer, more natural view. Then try zoom 2x to 5x (higher zooms depend on your phone) to pick the running man out of the crowd.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the Glico sign on one of the lines with some canal and neon around it, and keep your phone level so the buildings don't lean.
card.best_time: Come in the evening after sunset, when the signs light up. One guide suggests arriving at about 17:30, but the bridge will be busy then. After dark, switch on night mode and keep your elbows tucked against your body to hold the phone steady.
card.selfie_here: Do it on Ebisubashi, where the covered arcade ends, with the Glico running man sign across the canal behind you. Use the front camera, try zoom 0.5x so the sign fits over your shoulder, and hold the phone a little high.
card.ask_someone: If someone's friendly, ask them to take it from the opposite bank of the canal, facing the Glico sign, so you and the giant signs both fit in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: The bridge is very popular with photographers, so expect to share the railing and take your shot quickly.
card.challenge: Copy the running man's pose on the bridge and see if your photographer can get you and the sign in the same frame.
card.good_to_know: The name comes from a bridge: in 1622 a merchant called Shinsai Okada built a wooden bridge over the Nagahori-gawa canal, and the area took his name. The canal was filled in during 1964, but the name stayed. The arcade is roughly 600 m long and fully roofed, so it's handy for sheltering between shots.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Ebisubashi, the bridge at the south end of Shinsaibashi-suji where the arcade meets the Dotonbori canal. Face the Glico running man sign across the water; the arcade is behind you to the north.

card.hook: Picture a giant lion with its mouth wide open, stuffed full of wooden prayer plaques, and the city skyline peeking out behind it. Yes, this is a real shrine, and it's brilliant on a phone.
card.stand_here: Stand at Namba Yasaka Shrine in Osaka's Namba area, right on the phone icon, which sits at the lion itself. Walk to the side of the precinct and face the lion's right-side profile.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the side view, which can squeeze in some of the skyline. If space is tight, drop to zoom 0.5x to fit the whole head. Use zoom 2x for the open mouth and the plaques, so you don't have to get close to anyone.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the lion's head on one of the lines, and leave some space in front of its open mouth.
card.best_time: The side angle is usually less crowded than the head-on view, so shoot it first. Opening times vary between listings, so check the official site before you go.
card.selfie_here: Take your selfie at the front of the lion's head stage (the Ema-den), facing the shrine front, so the lion's bulk fills the frame behind you. Use the front camera, try zoom 0.5x to fit more in, and keep the lion over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand near the vermilion torii gate at the entrance, about 5 m back from the lion's face, while you stand in front of the lion.
card.rules_and_safety: This is a working shrine, so keep your voice down and be patient if prayers are under way. Photography is fine on the grounds, including the outside of the lion's head, but don't point your phone at people praying up close, and don't climb onto the lion's stage.
card.challenge: Get the side profile with the skyline in the top third, then step back and get the whole face too. Two lions for the price of one!
card.good_to_know: The lion's open mouth is filled with wooden ema prayer plaques. From the side you can see how deep the structure is, which the front view hides. It's a traditional shrine in a modern city, which is why the mix looks so good on a phone.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at Namba Yasaka Shrine in Osaka's Namba area, right on the phone icon, which sits at the lion itself. Walk to the side of the precinct and face the lion's right-side profile.

The selfie spots are inferred from guides that describe the front of the lion, the stairs up to it, and standing inside the mouth; no page specifically describes a selfie with the lion directly behind the subject, so treat these as the closest matches. The 'ask someone' spot is the torii-gate/entrance area; the guides say to stand back near the entrance for the best full-lion shot, but the exact spot is approximate. Sources disagree on the lion's dimensions (11 m vs 12 m wide) and the Osaka Tourism page contains details (lion orientation, light timing) that other sites don't confirm, so verify before relying on them. Photo-spot tips from user blogs also vary on the best time of day.

card.hook: Picture a covered shopping street with the tower sitting at the far end like the last dish on a very loud menu. Restaurant banners, lanterns and neon crowd in from both sides, and guides say this view beats the one from the observation deck.
card.stand_here: Stand at the southern end of 通天閣本通, the covered shopping street. The tower is about 35 m to the east of it. Face north along the arcade so the tower fills the far end. Street names can vary, so check the name on the map.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole arcade with its signs and lanterns. Switch to 1x for a cleaner view of the tower, or try 2x or higher (depending on your phone) to bring it closer to the busy signs.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the tower on the centre line, then tap the tower and drag the slider to make it a little darker so the neon keeps its colour.
card.best_time: Try about 4:00-6:00 PM, when the light is soft and the neon is already on. Most guides like late afternoon into blue hour, but one prefers morning light, so check on the day.
card.selfie_here: Head to the entrance arch of Tsutenkaku Hondori shopping street and stand so the tower is in view beyond it. A guide says the arch and tower make a good pair, and the arch is lit up at night. Use the front camera at 0.5x and let the arch and tower sit over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to stand at the crossing of Shinsekai-Hondori and Jan Jan Yokocho (about 100 metres northwest of the tower's base) while you stand with the tower behind you, framed by lanterns and shop signs, and check the exact spot on the map.
card.rules_and_safety: Always ask before photographing people or staff, since many are working. The area is busy, so shoot from the edge of an intersection rather than the middle of the flow.
card.challenge: Can you get the tower dead centre with a lantern glowing on each side, and not a single photobombing pedestrian? Be patient, the gap will come.
card.good_to_know: Tsūtenkaku means "Tower Reaching Heaven" and it stands 108 metres tall. The current tower opened in 1956 and is the second on the site. The first, built in 1912 and modelled on the Eiffel Tower and the Arc de Triomphe, was taken down after fire damage in 1943. Today the LED colours change every two months.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the southern end of 通天閣本通, the covered shopping street. The tower is about 35 m to the east of it. Face north along the arcade so the tower fills the far end. Street names can vary, so check the name on the map.

card.hook: Right behind the bright, noisy entertainment streets is a narrow stone lane glowing with red lanterns, and it feels like you've stepped into a different century. It's the best photo here, and you'll have to dodge a few people to get it.
card.stand_here: Stand at either end of Hozenji Yokocho and look straight down the lane. The temple is to the west, about 1 minute on foot.
card.zoom: Use zoom 1x for the lane so the walls and lanterns stretch away from you. Switch to zoom 0.5x for the temple and the mossy statue, where space is tight.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines to keep the walls straight, then tap a lantern and drag the slider so the shot gets a little darker and the reds don't wash out.
card.best_time: Dusk and blue hour are best, and the 30 minutes after sunset are the strongest. After rain the wet paving picks up the lantern glow. The moss on the statue looks freshest from January to May.
card.selfie_here: Try the wooden entrance gate of Hozenji Yokocho. Use the front camera, stand slightly to one side so the Japanese sign stays visible, and keep the entrance clear. Zoom 0.5x helps fit the gate over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Hand your phone to a passer-by at one of the alley approaches on either side of the temple and ask them to crouch low and use 0.5x so the lanterns overhead fit in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Keep the flash off, keep the approach to the Mizukake Fudo statue clear, and don't photograph people closely while they're praying. Check the signs at the temple, because photo rules there may differ from the lane.
card.challenge: Can you catch the whole lane with hardly anyone in it? Patience is the secret, so wait for your gap.
card.good_to_know: Hozen-ji was founded in 1637 and was long a favourite with actors and other performers. Almost everything was destroyed in the bombings of 1945, but the moss-covered statue Fudo Myoo, known as Mizukake Fudo, survived. Pouring water over it is a traditional good-luck gesture.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at either end of Hozenji Yokocho and look straight down the lane. The temple is to the west, about 1 minute on foot.

card.hook: You came to Osaka for the neon, and then a shopping centre hands you lawns, streams and a tiny waterfall on its roof. Namba Parks is a very green surprise right next to Namba Station.
card.stand_here: Stand on the top terraces of the rooftop garden (level 8 and up) and face out over the tower and the city. You want the green terraces in front of you, with Namba's rooftops and the Abeno Harukas tower behind.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the stepped garden and the full height of the complex in one shot. Switch to 1x for everyday pictures, then try 2x (or higher, if your phone has it) for streams, plants and people strolling the paths.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line up the terrace edges and the tower with them so the buildings stay straight, because any tilt shows.
card.best_time: Daylight shows off the greenery best, and softer morning or late-afternoon light is kinder than harsh midday sun. After dark the lit buildings look good too, so switch on night mode and hold the phone as still as you can.
card.selfie_here: Head to the top terrace of the rooftop garden, near the 8F Green Stage area, which is said to have the best photo angles. Use the front camera, try 0.5x so more of the garden fits in, and keep the terraces and city over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to shoot you from the canyon viewpoints along the 4th-floor walkway, so the building and garden end up behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos are generally fine in the common areas and the rooftop garden, but some individual shops don't allow them inside. Check the official site before you go for garden access and any closures.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot that shows how big the place is, then find a stream, pond or rock group and make it look like you're miles from the city.
card.good_to_know: Namba Parks was built on the site of the old Osaka Stadium. Jon Jerde designed it as a green break in a very dense part of the city. The garden climbs through eight levels to the 9th floor, and there are about 120 shops inside.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the top terraces of the rooftop garden (level 8 and up) and face out over the tower and the city. You want the green terraces in front of you, with Namba's rooftops and the Abeno Harukas tower behind.

card.hook: Don't come to Amerikamura for a postcard view. Come for the crowd, the signs and the shops squeezed shoulder to shoulder. It's more about atmosphere than scenery, and that's the fun of it.
card.stand_here: Stand at Triangle Park (三角公園), the small concrete plaza at the heart of Amerikamura. The phone icon on the map marks the spot, so there's no distance to walk. Face the shopfronts and keep them behind the people.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the plaza and the shops around it. Go to 1x for people and street scenes. Try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the little Statue of Liberty replica on a rooftop.
card.make_it_pop: Tap a bright sign, then slide it a touch darker so the neon and shop signs don't wash out.
card.best_time: Weekend afternoons into the evening are busiest, which is great for atmosphere. For a clear shot of a mural or shopfront, a weekday morning is usually quieter.
card.selfie_here: Sit on the concrete steps in Triangle Park, face the front camera towards you, and let the busy shopping street fill the background. Zoom 0.5x gets more of the scene in behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: If you're photographing people up close, ask them first. Triangle Park has steps and low walls but no ramps, so step-free access may be difficult.
card.challenge: Spot the tiny Statue of Liberty on a rooftop and get it in a shot with a crowd below it. Look up!
card.good_to_know: Amerikamura, or Ame-mura, began in the 1970s, when warehouses here sold imported American clothes, jeans and second-hand records. The 1983 "Peace on Earth" mural by Seitaro Kuroda is a popular subject, but we can't point to its exact wall, so keep an eye out as you wander. Shopfronts and street art change over time, so don't rely on old photos to find things.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at Triangle Park (三角公園), the small concrete plaza at the heart of Amerikamura. The phone icon on the map marks the spot, so there's no distance to walk. Face the shopfronts and keep them behind the people.

card.hook: There's a giant red whale hanging inside a shopping centre in Osaka, and it's the easiest photo you'll take all day. The big red Ferris wheel gets the fame, but the whale is the one you can shoot from close range.
card.stand_here: Stand in the HEP FIVE atrium, just inside the entrance, right where the phone icon on the map is. Face the red whale so the route of the Ferris wheel gondolas shows up behind it.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the whale. If the whale and the wheel route won't both fit, tap 0.5x.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the whale, then slide the brightness down a little (darker) if the bright background washes out the red.
card.best_time: Just wait for a clear gap in front of the whale in the atrium. For the outside view of the wheel, daytime with a clear sky shows the red best.
card.selfie_here: Go to the atrium just inside the 1st-floor main entrance and pose under the hanging red whale and its calf. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and let the whale hang over your shoulder. The Ferris wheel won't be in this one.
card.rules_and_safety: The whale is inside a shopping building and the wheel is a separate ride, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Get the whole whale in the frame, with the wheel route behind it and not a single stranger walking through. Patience wins this one.
card.good_to_know: HEP FIVE is a shopping building in Osaka with a big red Ferris wheel rising above it. The red of the whale and the red of the wheel tie the picture together, so it reads clearly even on a small screen. The wheel was reported closed from late October 2025 to the end of April 2026, so check the official site if you want to ride it or see it turning.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in the HEP FIVE atrium, just inside the entrance, right where the phone icon on the map is. Face the red whale so the route of the Ferris wheel gondolas shows up behind it.

card.hook: Here's a surprise: right in the middle of Osaka's city bustle sits a 3 km sandbank with rose beds, bridges and museums on it. Don't hunt for one perfect shot. Treat it like a stroll with a camera.
card.stand_here: Stand about 210 m north-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, near 阪神高速1号環状線, and face south-west. Keep the river in the frame, because the water is what makes it look like an island.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x for the river, the sky and the long line of buildings. Switch to 1x for a single bridge or building, then try 2x or 5x (if your phone has them) for a roofline, a rose bed or the far bank.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the river's edge on a lower line with buildings or trees above it, and tap the sky then slide to darker if it looks washed out.
card.best_time: Late afternoon to early evening usually gives softer light on the water and buildings. Earlier in the day it's quieter, so the promenade is easier to shoot without people in the frame. After dark, check that the water is showing reflections before you shoot.
card.selfie_here: Head into the Nakanoshima Park Rose Garden and use the front camera with the Osaka City Central Public Hall's dome behind you. Hold the phone a little low and let the dome peek over your shoulder, with the roses in front of it.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to take your photo on the pedestrian walkway of Naniwabashi Bridge (the Lion Bridge), so the lit-up Public Hall and its reflection in the Tosabori River fill the frame behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The island and riverside walkways are public space, but check access details locally before you go. One guide says photography permission is needed for the Public Hall's exterior, so check before you shoot it. Stand back from the water's edge and hold the phone with both hands.
card.challenge: Find a spot where a railing or a tree sits in the foreground, water fills the lower third, and the buildings stay perfectly upright.
card.good_to_know: Nakanoshima is a long, narrow sandbank about 3 km from end to end and roughly 50 hectares. It splits the old Yodo river into two channels, the Tosabori and the Dōjima. The island holds Osaka's city hall, the Nakanoshima Library, the National Museum of Art and the Science Museum.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand about 210 m north-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, near 阪神高速1号環状線, and face south-west. Keep the river in the frame, because the water is what makes it look like an island.

Only one selfie spot was confirmed with the landmark behind the visitor; the other sources describe photographing the building rather than selfies in front of it, so I did not add a second spot. The Naniwabashi Bridge recommendation is for a photo of the hall at night, not a stated selfie position. One source says photography permission is required for the Public Hall's exterior, which other sources do not mention, so check before shooting. Pages mention tripods only as shooting advice, not as rules, so no tripod or selfie-stick rule is listed. Rose garden hours are listed as roughly 9:00–21:00 on one page, and roses bloom in May and October according to others.

card.hook: Surprise: this big, clean-lined building sits on the site of the old Naniwa Palace, so you're photographing the new next to a very, very old story. All those repeating shapes on the facade make it a great phone subject.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the Osaka Museum of History, where the phone icon sits on the map. Step back as far as the space allows and face the building so it fits in your frame.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to squeeze in the full height, then go to 1x for a more natural look with less stretching at the edges. Want a close-up of the facade pattern or part of the atrium? Try 2x, or higher if your phone has it.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on your gridlines and line the building's vertical edges up with them, because a tilted phone makes tall walls lean.
card.best_time: Daytime in good light shows the facade most clearly. Early or late in the day the light is softer, though that depends on the weather and season.
card.selfie_here: Head to the life-sized Hoenzaka warehouse replica outside the museum, which is described as a popular photo stop. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and check your screen, because we couldn't confirm the museum fits behind you from there.
card.ask_someone: Try the southwest corner of Osaka Castle Park, which is across from the museum, and ask a passer-by to take your photo there with the museum and the NHK building in the view across from you.
card.rules_and_safety: Selfie sticks and flash aren't allowed inside the museum. Photography is fine for personal use in the permanent exhibition, but some display cases have no-flash signs, so check the official site before you go in.
card.challenge: Find the straightest, most perfectly lined-up shot of the facade you can, then sneak the link to the NHK building into the edge of the frame.
card.good_to_know: The museum opened in 2001 and tells Osaka's story across four floors, starting with the Naniwa Palace period. Down below ground you can see remains of a palace warehouse, walls and water supply facilities. It was designed by César Pelli & Associates with Nihon Sekkei, the same team behind the NHK Osaka Broadcasting Center next door, and an atrium joins the two.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand right at the Osaka Museum of History, where the phone icon sits on the map. Step back as far as the space allows and face the building so it fits in your frame.

The Hoenzaka replica is named and called a photo spot, but its exact position relative to the museum and whether the museum fits in frame are unverified. A tsunagujapan.com snippet about 'Shinshigino Bridge' appears to belong to a different spot and was not used. Tripod rules come from two sources that differ slightly: one bans them outright, the other says they may be restricted.

card.hook: Picture a stone lion on a bridge in the foreground, with a red-brick hall glowing behind it across the water. That's Osaka City Central Public Hall, and the lion makes the photo look like a postcard.
card.stand_here: Stand at the Nakanoshima end of Naniwabashi (難波橋), about 340 m to the east of the hall. Face west across the Dojima River and line up one of the bridge's lion statues in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x so the lion and the hall both fit. Try zoom 0.5x if you want the lion big in the foreground, but keep it a little back from the edges so it doesn't stretch. Zoom 2x gets you a tighter shot of the roof and front across the river.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the lion low in one corner and the hall on the opposite third, and hold your phone level so the walls stay straight.
card.best_time: Evening is best, when the hall is lit and the river adds reflections. Morning also works, because the sun is behind you when you look west. Seasonal light displays aren't permanent, so check the schedule first.
card.selfie_here: Head to the riverside path in Nakanoshima Park and turn so the hall is directly behind you. Use the front camera (or zoom 0.5x if your phone has it) and keep the hall over your shoulder. Sunset and night, when it's lit, are the moments to go for.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by on the Naniwabashi (Lion Bridge) walkway to take it, with you in the shot and the lit hall and its reflection behind you. The exact spot on the bridge isn't fixed, so check the framing when you arrive.
card.rules_and_safety: The bridge and surroundings are open public space, but photography rules can vary, so check the official site before you go. Shooting inside needs permission, and for any commercial or pre-wedding shoot, confirm locally.
card.challenge: Get the lion and the hall in one shot, with the lion small and low in a corner and the red brick still easy to spot. Bonus points if the lion looks like it's guarding the building.
card.good_to_know: Building began in 1913 and finished in 1918, paid for by a gift of 1 million yen from the broker Einosuke Iwamoto. The style is Renaissance Revival. After a long refurbishment that began in 1999, including work to make it stronger in earthquakes, it reopened in November 2002 and was named a cultural asset of national importance that December.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the Nakanoshima end of Naniwabashi (難波橋), about 340 m to the east of the hall. Face west across the Dojima River and line up one of the bridge's lion statues in front of you.

selfie_spots.why: Sources describe the riverbanks as the main vantage point for the hall, especially at sunset and at night when it is lit.

card.hook: Here's a gate that doesn't make you crane your neck. Step back and the whole thing fits in your screen with the lines standing nice and straight.
card.stand_here: Stand about 30 m west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face east. The gate is a 1-minute walk from there.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the whole gate, the ground in front and a bit of sky. Use 0.5x only if you step closer and can't fit it all in, then try 2x or more (depending on your phone) for the details.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on gridlines, put the gate on the middle vertical line, then tap the gate and slide to darker if the sky looks washed out.
card.best_time: Early morning usually means fewer people in your shot. The sun moves through the day, so check how the light hits the gate when you arrive and shift your spot if you need to.
card.selfie_here: Stand on the stone bridge over the outer moat, just outside the gate, with the gate behind you. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, and hold it a little low so the gate sits over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask your helper to stand to one side of the gate's front, not in the middle, so the whole gate still fits in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Access may vary, so check local information before you go.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot, then wait for a stranger to wander past so the gate looks properly big. Bonus points if they have no idea they're in it.
card.good_to_know: Otemon Gate works well as a straightforward travel photo: a strong structure, a clear way in and room to step back. You can fit the whole gateway in without tilting your phone up. For the history, local information is the best place to check before you go.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand about 30 m west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face east. The gate is a 1-minute walk from there.

selfie_spots.why: Visitors who stand in front of the gate get the classic frontal view of the castle, and the gate reads clearly as the backdrop.

card.hook: The worst place to photograph a bridge is on it. Back off a little and you can see the whole sweep of it, from one side of the gap to the other.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon on the map, about 70 m east of the subject, and face west towards Gokurakubashi Bridge. Fancy a closer second shot? It's about 1 minute on foot towards the bridge.
card.zoom: Start at 1x so you get the whole bridge and a bit of its surroundings. Then try 2x-5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the railings, or any people crossing. Save 0.5x for when you've stepped closer and want a dramatic sweep.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines and line the bridge up along a horizontal one so it sits nice and level.
card.best_time: Early morning or later in the afternoon usually gives softer light. You're facing west, so a low evening sun may be in front of you. If so, tap the bridge and check the result, then go a bit darker if the sky is too bright.
card.selfie_here: Try the spot between Gokurakubashi Bridge and the Gozabune boat launch, in front of the ticket place for the castle moat boat ride, just short of the bridge. Use the front camera, try 0.5x to fit more in, and check on screen that the bridge is over your shoulder. That's not guaranteed from this spot, so a quick test shot helps.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by on the eastern bank of the inner moat, ideally in morning light, to shoot with the bridge in view while you stand in the picture.
card.rules_and_safety: Access details aren't given, so check the local signs on site.
card.challenge: Take two frames of the same view, one standing and one slightly crouched, and see which one makes the bridge look better.
card.good_to_know: This Gokurakubashi Bridge is in the Osaka Castle grounds (Chuo-ku), not the Gokurakubashi station in Koya-san. The walk between the two points is very short, so you can take your time.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the phone icon on the map, about 70 m east of the subject, and face west towards Gokurakubashi Bridge. Fancy a closer second shot? It's about 1 minute on foot towards the bridge.
